implementation_notes: The pattern's home form: wrap only the single call, catch only the narrowest checked exception it declares, name the caught variable `ignored` so the intent is explicit, and put the justification in a comment next to the handler. Choose it when the mute is a one-off; a helper is justified once the same mute repeats at several call sites.
pitfalls: `catch (Exception ignored)` defeats the idiom: catch the specific checked type the call declares, or the mute absorbs every failure the method body can produce.
An empty catch is exactly what analyzers and reviewers look for, so the `ignored` name plus the comment are the artefact that distinguishes a decision from a bug.
Muting inside a finally block or a try-with-resources close can mask the original exception; use the suppressed-exception information (getSuppressed()) when both can occur.

variants.name: Reusable Mute helper over a CheckedRunnable
variants.idiom_name: static void mute(CheckedRunnable r) { try { r.run(); } catch (SpecificException ignored) { } }
variants.implementation_notes: Java 8 lambdas let the mute be written once: declare a functional interface whose method throws and a helper that runs it inside the narrow catch - the catalog's own Mute.loggedMute form, with the logging kept inside the helper so the ignored failure still leaves a breadcrumb. Method references then make call sites read as ordinary statements. Use it when many call sites share the same ignorable failure type; keep the inline form when each justification differs.
pitfalls: A helper that catches Throwable, or logs NullPointerException-like programming errors at ERROR next to real IO conditions, turns the mute into an error sink.
Lambdas and method references capture the enclosing instance, so a mute helper registered on a long-lived object can keep state alive - a leak class the inline form does not have.
One shared helper for many call sites erases the per-site justification; make the helper take a reason string or keep the reasoning at the call site.
